merge_log.llm_reason: Both statements describe the same normative requirement: server returns 257 reply with directory name upon successful MKD command.
Both statements describe the same requirement: server sends 226/250 reply and user-PI should wait before issuing new transfer command.
Both statements describe the same normative requirement: the server must close the data connection immediately after transfer when EOF is not signaled by connection close.
Both statements describe the same normative requirement: server closes control connection after QUIT with all transfers and replies complete.
Both statements describe the same normative requirement that the user-PI initiates the full-duplex control connection to the server.

resolution_log.llm_reason: The statement is a backward-compatibility declaration about implementation conformance across spec versions, not tied to any protocol state transition.

The spec defines this under terminology/pathname as a general convention applying to all file transfers regardless of protocol state: 'Each user must follow the file naming conventions of the file systems involved in the transfer.'

The spec states this as a general note about data connection capability ('It ought to also be noted that the data connection may be used for simultaneous sending and receiving'), not tied to any specific state transition.

The spec declares a set of minimum capability requirements (TYPE, MODE, STRUCTURE, COMMANDS) that all servers must support regardless of protocol state, making this a global build-time/capability constraint rather than a state transition.
The default transfer parameters (TYPE ASCII Non-print, MODE Stream, STRU File) are declarative configuration requirements applying to all hosts regardless of protocol state.

The spec states this convention applies to both server- and user-processes generally during connection setup, with no specific state transition implied, making it a global protocol constraint on Telnet convention compliance.
The spec states servers are under no obligation to provide command line editing as a general capability declaration about server behavior, not tied to any specific state transition.
The spec states this as a universal implementation requirement ('all FTP implementation must support') independent of any particular protocol state.
The spec states this recommendation applies whenever the system spontaneously has a message to send, with no specific state context — it applies across all protocol states.

The spec states reply code semantics and command-reply sequences must be strictly adhered to across all commands and states, making this a global protocol constraint independent of any specific state transition.
The rule about discarding trailing zeros applies to the page data format during any transfer, not tied to a specific state transition.
The statement is a general advisory about pathname compatibility between MKD and CWD across different OS implementations, not tied to any specific state transition.

This is a general advisory note about pathname suitability across platforms, not tied to a specific state transition; the spec recommends the 257 response as the solution, making this a global protocol constraint on MKD argument handling.
